analysis.one_liner: Overrides state laws to limit what people can recover when defective products injure them.
analysis.headline: A Senate bill to cap damages and limit lawsuits over defective products drew 35 Republican cosponsors, got one committee hearing, and died without ever coming to a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have replaced the 50 states' product liability rules with a single federal set of rules for lawsuits over defective products. It capped punitive damages, ended joint liability for pain-and-suffering awards, set strict deadlines for suing, gave sellers near-total protection, and virtually eliminated lawsuits against companies that supply raw materials for medical implants. It would have primarily benefited manufacturers, sellers, insurers, and implant material suppliers, while people injured by defective products would recover less and face shorter windows to sue. The Senate Commerce Committee held one hearing and never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Product manufacturers, sellers, and liability insurers gain the most: uniform national rules that reduce the size and number of damage awards, cap punitive damages at no more than the greater of twice compensatory damages or a fixed dollar ceiling [S3], and let each defendant pay only its own percentage share of pain-and-suffering awards [S3]. Companies that supply raw materials and components for medical implants would be shielded from suit entirely unless their materials violated a written contract specification [S3]. Sellers that did not make the product would face liability only if a claimant proved they were careless, broke their own warranty, or acted intentionally [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Manufacturers, sellers, insurers, and biomaterials suppliers

how_it_helps.text: Caps punitive damages at no more than the greater of two times compensatory damages or $250,000, and requires a claimant to prove 'conscious, flagrant indifference to the rights or safety of others' by clear and convincing evidence before any punitive award [S3].
Ends joint liability for noneconomic losses, so each defendant pays only its assigned percentage; if a responsible company is insolvent or untouchable, the injured person absorbs the shortfall [S3].
Sets a uniform two-year deadline to sue from when harm is discovered and a 15-year cutoff for durable goods, overriding longer state deadlines [S3].
Gives defendants a complete defense if the injured person was intoxicated and more than 50 percent responsible for the accident, and reduces damages by the share attributable to product misuse [S3].

Exempts biomaterials suppliers from implant lawsuits unless they were the actual manufacturer or seller or furnished materials that failed contractual specifications, and lets them dismiss suits early with limited discovery [S3].

analysis.who_pays: People injured or killed by defective products. They would recover less in pain-and-suffering awards, face a shorter window to file, lose full recovery when one responsible party cannot pay, and lose nearly all recourse against the companies that supply implant materials. Because the bill preempts state law, states with stronger consumer protections would be overridden [S3].

drawbacks.text: The strongest objection: injured people would recover less, particularly through the punitive damages cap and the end of joint liability — in a case against several defendants, any insolvent one leaves the injured person unpaid for the rest [S3].

The two-year federal deadline could expire before some latent harms are discovered or diagnosed, since it runs from when a person discovered or 'should have' discovered both the harm and its cause [S3].
An honest supporter would acknowledge that the bill overrides the tort systems all 50 states have built for themselves, including jury-based damages rules that state legislatures chose not to cap.
The biomaterials shield leaves an implant maker as the only realistic target even when a raw material itself was defective, as long as the material met the written spec the supplier published [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Supporters argued that inconsistent state rules and unpredictable awards raised prices and pushed some implant material suppliers out of the market [S3]. The bill's uniformity and the biomaterials provisions had a genuine rationale. But its main effect is a broad transfer of risk away from manufacturers and insurers and onto injured people: lower punitive awards, no joint liability, tighter deadlines, and preemption of state law. The protections for careless sellers and the near-total immunity for biomaterials suppliers go well beyond what the supply-shortage problem required, since suppliers who violated written specifications could still be sued only with difficulty.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which held one hearing in March 1997, never voted on it, and it died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Senator John Ashcroft introduced the bill on January 21, 1997, with 34 cosponsors, all Republicans [S4][S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day [S5].
The committee held hearings on March 4, 1997 — the only committee action the bill ever received [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill never reached the Senate floor and expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 1999 [S5][S1].
A nearly identical product liability bill had passed both chambers in 1996 and was vetoed by President Clinton, which shadowed this attempt [widely reported].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Injured consumers kept the state tort systems they already had, and manufacturers, insurers, and biomaterials suppliers got nothing — though they also lost nothing, since existing law remained unchanged. States retained full control over product liability rules.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Injured consumers kept existing state remedies

for.name: Sen. John Ashcroft
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Product Liability Reform Act of 1997 and delivered introductory remarks.

for.name: 35 of 55 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Democrat cosponsored it.

for.name: Business and manufacturing lobbies
for.role: National business groups supporting federal tort limits
for.what_they_did: Backed federal product liability limits as a long-standing legislative priority throughout the 1990s.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Held one hearing on March 4, 1997, then never reported the bill or scheduled a vote, letting it die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: President Bill Clinton
against.what_they_did: Vetoed the predecessor product liability bill passed by Congress in 1996, establishing White House opposition to federal product liability limits.

against.name: Trial lawyers' associations
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal caps on damages and product liability limits throughout the 1990s debate.

sides.party_line_note: All 35 cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat sponsored or cosponsored the bill, and it died in a committee chaired by a Republican cosponsor without a vote.

industries.note: The bill cuts the size and number of damage awards against them, caps punitive damages, ends joint liability, and gives non-manufacturer sellers near-total protection. Injured people would recover less, so the industry's gain comes directly at the public's cost.

Predictable, capped awards reduce insurer payouts, and the bill gives workers' compensation insurers a guaranteed right to recover benefits from manufacturers and sellers. The savings flow to insurers rather than to injured workers, whose damages can be reduced by the insurer's recovery.

industries.industry: Biomaterials suppliers (raw material and component makers for implants)
industries.note: The bill grants them near-immunity from implant lawsuits, which suppliers said would restore supplies of materials that some had stopped selling for medical devices. The trade-off is that patients harmed by a defective material could rarely reach the supplier that made it.

Uniform limits, capped awards, and early dismissal procedures for biomaterials suits would sharply reduce viable cases and fees. In this bill, the trial bar's interest in keeping cases viable runs alongside injured people's interest in full recovery.
